name: Unvalidated Input
description: Information from web requests is not validated before being used by a web application. Attackers can use these flaws to attack backend components through a web application.
preventions: Validate all input from untrusted sources.
Reject invalid input; do not sanitize it.
Use an allow-list approach for validation.

name: Broken Access Control
description: Restrictions on what authenticated users are allowed to do are often not properly enforced. Attackers can exploit these flaws to access other users' accounts, view sensitive files, or use unauthorized functions.
preventions: Implement access control checks server-side.
Deny by default.
Log access control failures.

name: Broken Authentication and Session Management
description: Account credentials and session tokens are often not properly protected. Attackers who can compromise passwords, keys, or authentication tokens can assume other users' identities.
preventions: Use strong session tokens generated server-side.
Invalidate sessions after logout and timeout.
Protect credentials in transit and at rest.

name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: XSS flaws occur when an application sends user-supplied data to a browser without proper validation or encoding. Attackers can execute scripts in the victim's browser which can hijack user sessions or redirect the user to malicious sites.
preventions: Encode all user-controlled output.
Use Content Security Policy (CSP).
Validate input against a strict allow-list.

name: Buffer Overflow
description: Web application components in some languages that do not properly validate input can be crashed and in some cases used to take control of a process. These components can include CGI, libraries, drivers, and web application server components.
preventions: Use memory-safe languages.
Validate and bound-check all input.
Use compiler protections like stack canaries and ASLR.

name: Injection Flaws
description: Injection flaws allow attackers to relay malicious code through a web application to another system. These attacks include system calls, the use of external programs via shell commands, SQL injection, LDAP, XPath, and other injection attacks.
preventions: Use parameterized queries and prepared statements.
Validate and encode all user input.
Apply the principle of least privilege on the database.

name: Improper Error Handling
description: Error conditions arising in software are not handled properly, causing errors to be returned to users that can reveal technical details such as stack traces, database dumps, and error codes.
preventions: Use generic error messages for users.
Log detailed errors server-side only.
Handle all exceptions consistently.

name: Insecure Storage
description: Web applications commonly use cryptographic functions to protect information and credentials. Developers frequently make mistakes implementing these functions, such as using weak algorithms or failing to rotate keys properly.
preventions: Use strong, up-to-date cryptographic algorithms.
Protect cryptographic keys.
Do not store sensitive data unless absolutely necessary.

name: Application Denial of Service
description: Attackers can consume web application resources to the point where other legitimate users can no longer access or use the application. Attackers can also lock users out of their accounts or even cause the entire application to fail.
preventions: Implement rate limiting.
Set resource consumption limits per user.
Use CAPTCHA where appropriate.

name: Insecure Configuration Management
description: Having a strong server configuration standard is critical to a secure web application. Servers have many configuration options that affect security, and default configurations are often not restrictive enough.
preventions: Remove unnecessary features, components, and documentation.
Apply security hardening to all servers.
Keep all software up to date with patches.
